title: American Air Rifle Champion Credits Training at New Delhi's Topgun Academy for Title Win
excerpt: Jeff Browning won the U.S. National 10-meter air rifle championship after training for two years at India's Topgun Shooting Academy, highlighting the country's growing role in global competitive shooting.
body:
• Jeff Browning won the U.S. National 10-meter air rifle championship after training for approximately two years at the Topgun Shooting Academy in New Delhi, India.
  • The academy, founded by Shimon Sharif — the first rifle shooter from Delhi to represent India at the ISSF World Cup — has become a training ground for international competitors.
  • During the COVID-19 pandemic, Topgun hosted virtual competitions that attracted members of the U.S. Olympic shooting team, including Tokyo gold medalist William Shaner and silver medalist Lucas Kozeniesky.
  • The story highlights India's growing role as a global hub for competitive shooting sports, with world-class facilities drawing athletes from abroad.

When Jeff Browning stepped onto the firing line at Camp Perry, Ohio to claim the Leatherneck Trophy at the U.S. National 10-meter air rifle championship, he brought with him something unusual: two years of training at a shooting academy in New Delhi, India. His victory underscores an unlikely but growing trend — American competitive shooters traveling to India to sharpen their skills.

Training at Topgun

Browning, who has been competing in air rifle events since 2012, trained at the Topgun Shooting Academy, a facility in New Delhi that has quietly built a reputation as one of the best-equipped private shooting academies in Asia. The academy was founded by Shimon Sharif, who holds the distinction of being the first rifle shooter from Delhi to represent India at an ISSF World Cup.

"National 10-meter air rifle championship, he brought with him something unusual: two years of training at a shooting academy in New Delhi, India."

Under Sharif's coaching and using the academy's international-standard facilities, Browning honed his technique before returning to the United States for the national championships. He also won the men's 10-meter air rifle event at the Topgun Cup, a two-day international competition held at the academy that drew notable participants from multiple countries.

India's Growing Shooting Sports Infrastructure

India's rise in competitive shooting has been one of the quieter success stories in global sports. The country has produced Olympic and World Championship medalists in recent years, and the infrastructure supporting the sport has expanded rapidly. Purpose-built academies like Topgun offer electronic targets, climate-controlled ranges, and coaching ecosystems that rival facilities in traditional shooting powerhouses like Germany, South Korea, and the United States.

The Topgun Academy gained international visibility during the COVID-19 pandemic, when Sharif organized virtual competitions that attracted members of the U.S. Olympic shooting team. William Shaner, who went on to win gold in the 10-meter air rifle at the Tokyo Olympics, and Lucas Kozeniesky, who won silver in the mixed team event, both participated in these remote competitions hosted from New Delhi.

A Two-Way Exchange

Browning's story illustrates a maturing two-way exchange in competitive shooting. For decades, Indian shooters traveled to European and American facilities for advanced training. Now the flow is beginning to reverse, with international athletes recognizing the quality of coaching and infrastructure available in India.

The Delhi State Open Shooting Competition and national-level meets have become proving grounds for the academy's students, who have won numerous medals. Several of Sharif's trainees have competed at ISSF Junior World Championships, including Paarth Makhija and Shaurya Sarin, who medaled at the 2023 Junior Worlds in Lima, Peru.

What It Means

Competitive shooting remains a niche sport in most countries, but India's investment in grassroots infrastructure is paying dividends. The National Rifle Association of India (NRAI) has expanded access to ranges and coaching programs, and private academies like Topgun are filling gaps that public facilities sometimes cannot. For an American champion to credit Indian training as a key factor in his success signals that the country's shooting sports ecosystem has reached a level of credibility that extends well beyond its borders.
